In a pointed email, Elon Musk issued an ultimatum: “Either go do something on your own or continue with OpenAI as a nonprofit.” 

He warned he would stop funding the organization unless they firmly committed, saying he refused to “provide free funding for you to create a startup.” Sam Altman replied the next day: “I remain enthusiastic about the non-profit structure!”

That same month, OpenAI President Greg Brockman wrote in his private diary: “I cannot believe that we committed to non-profit if three months later we’re doing b-corp… then it was a lie.”

These exchanges underscore the core of Musk’s federal lawsuit (4:24-cv-04722-YGR). 

He alleges that Altman and Brockman secured his ~$38 million in early donations by promising to uphold OpenAI’s founding nonprofit mission — building safe AGI for humanity’s benefit — only to secretly plan a shift to a for-profit B-corp structure months later. 

Musk is seeking to unwind the conversion, remove Altman and Brockman from leadership, and secure damages.

The contrast between Altman’s public reassurance and Brockman’s private skepticism is now front and center in court — powerful evidence in a case that could reshape OpenAI’s future.

A new prompt inside the car lets drivers quickly report when Full Self-Driving misses turns or picks the wrong route. It’s a small change, but it puts real-world feedback right into Tesla’s data loop.

Navigation has been one of the weaker spots for FSD, especially in complex city driving. This move suggests Tesla is tightening the feedback cycle to fix those edge cases faster.

The more drivers respond, the faster the system learns.
